title: Diagnoses are rising in England and the US
context: Recorded depression is rising on both sides of the Atlantic, and so are ADHD diagnoses in US children. A diagnosis count rises when more people are ill, and also when more people are assessed.
ask: Is the rise in illness, in awareness, or in who gets assessed?

series.label: England: depression register
series.about: Adults on GP depression registers in England (financial years, plotted at their first year). It counts people diagnosed and not marked resolved.

series.label: US: ever told depression
series.about: US adults who say a doctor or other health professional has ever told them they have a depressive disorder (BRFSS, median of the states).

series.label: Colorado: ever told depression
series.about: The same question asked of adults in Colorado.

series.label: US children: ever told ADHD
series.about: US children under 18 whose parents say a doctor has ever told them the child has ADHD (National Health Interview Survey).

numbers.text: England's depression register, 5.8% to 14.3% of adults, 2012/13 to 2024/25.
US adults ever told they have depression, 2011 to 2025. Colorado: 17.6% to 22.3%.
US children ever told they have ADHD, 2019 to 2025.

caption: England: adults on GP depression registers (financial years, plotted at their first year). US and Colorado: adults ever told by a health professional they have depression (BRFSS, median of states). US children: ever told ADHD (NHIS). Different measures: compare direction, not level.
caveats: England's register keeps everyone diagnosed since April 2006 unless marked resolved, so it grows even when new diagnoses are flat.
The US has no national GP register; 'ever told' survey answers are the nearest equivalent.
There is no US equivalent of England's psychosis register.
